audits.mathematicalReason: Let the cube's edge length be s>0. Applying the Pythagorean theorem across a face and then through the cube gives PQ²=2s²+s²=3s². Thus s²=a²/3, and the surface area is 6s²=2a². The proposed surface-area scope and supporting Pythagorean method are defensible.

audits.mathematicalReason: Draw AC and BD. Since AD is a diameter, triangles ABD and ACD are right, and BD=√(16−1)=√15. Let T be the foot of the perpendicular from B to AC. Since AB=BC, T is the midpoint of AC and ∠BAT=∠BCA=∠BDA. Hence triangles ABT and DAB are similar, giving AT=BD/4=√15/4. Thus AC=√15/2 and CD=√(16−15/4)=7/2. The trigonometric route also works: with α=∠BDA, sin α=1/4. Inscribed-angle and isosceles relations give ∠ABC=180°−2α, so the cyclic-quadrilateral property gives ∠ADC=2α. Consequently CD=4 cos(2α)=4(1−2/16)=7/2. Both proposed routes are valid alternatives.

audits.mathematicalReason: External tangency makes every distance between circle centers equal to 6, so the centers form an equilateral triangle. Each enclosing common tangent is parallel to the corresponding center-to-center segment because its two perpendicular radii have equal length. Therefore the outer triangle is equilateral. At each outer vertex, the adjacent circle center bisects the 60° angle. A perpendicular radius of length 3 is opposite 30°, so the hypotenuse is 6 and the tangent leg is √(36−9)=3√3. Along each outer side, the two circle-contact points are 6 apart. Thus each side is 6+6√3 and the perimeter is 18+18√3.

figureEvidence.fact: The triangle encloses all three circles. Its base is a common outer tangent to the lower two circles, and each sloping side is a common outer tangent to the upper circle and one lower circle.

audits.mathematicalReason: Write u=BC and v=AB, with AC=1. In triangle CDE, ∠CDE=80°. AA similarity between triangles CDE and CED gives CD=CE=u/2; this uses the supplied similarity scopes rather than an unverified isosceles-converse scope. Through B draw BG parallel to DE, meeting AC at G. Triangles CBG and CED are similar, so CG=2CD=u and AG=1−u. Also ∠ABG=20° and ∠AGB=100°, so triangles ABG and ACB are similar, giving v²=1−u. The cosine law at A gives u²=1+v²−v, hence v=2−u−u²=(1−u)(u+2)=v²(u+2). Since v>0, v(u+2)=1. Let Δ be the area of ABC. Its altitude to AC is v sin60°, so Δ=√3v/4. Base-height ratios give [CDE]/Δ=(CD/AC)(CE/BC)=u/4. Therefore Δ+2[CDE]=Δ(1+u/2)=√3v(u+2)/8=√3/8. This supplies a complete corrected similarity-based mapping.

audits.mathematicalReason: The initial order gives 0<x<y<z. Rotation preserves the prospective triangle's side lengths x, y−x, and z−y. Its three strict triangle inequalities simplify to z−x>x, giving x<z/2 (I); x+z−y>y−x, giving y<x+z/2 (II); and y>z−y, giving y>z/2. Thus III is not merely unnecessary: it contradicts the third required inequality. Strict inequalities are essential because the triangle must have positive area.
